description: The fact that so many creative minds and space enthusiasts are coming together in one place means that great things can happen.
summary:
Dr. Farmer is an agricultural intelligence platform that transforms NASA satellite data and live weather information into practical insights for farmers and researchers.

The platform allows farmers to outline their fields on interactive 2D and 3D maps, analyze four satellite-derived variables (soil moisture, solar radiation, water retention, and soil temperature), and monitor six real-time weather metrics. Based on this information, it aims to support crop selection, yield improvement, and soil-regenerating crop rotations. It also connects farmers and researchers through an open science portal, where growers can share field observations and researchers can access local data and contribute scientific insights.

Dr. Farmer addresses the gap between complex NASA Earth observation datasets and their practical application in agriculture. By making this information accessible without requiring expensive field hardware, the project helps farmers make better-informed decisions while providing researchers with valuable ground-level observations.

This is especially important in regions facing drought, unpredictable weather, and soil degradation. Dr. Farmer aims to support more resilient agricultural practices through accessible satellite intelligence and collaboration.
details:
1. Executive Summary and Relevance to the Challenge

Agriculture uses around 70% of freshwater withdrawn globally, while food demand could increase by up to 60%, which could affect some farmers due to water waste.

Dr.Farm is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform created by Artemis Squad. Upon logging in and delineating the exact hectares of their plot on a 2D/3D map, farmers and researchers receive dynamic diagnostics on photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), UV radiation, water vapor, temperature, effective rainfall, and root-zone moisture. Thus, it answers a key decision for the farmer: “to irrigate or not to irrigate today, even if it just rained?” and for the researcher: “Which crops are having difficulty growing?”, in addition to recommending soil-regenerating rotations—with an estimated water savings of 30%.

2. Problem Statement: Climate Risk in Jalisco and the “Last Mile” Gap

The agro-environmental diagnosis of Jalisco, Mexico—a national agri-food powerhouse—reflects the critical challenges agriculture faces in the wake of climate change:

  • Rainfed dependence and water deficit: 83% of the state's agricultural area (1.42 million ha) depends on seasonal rainfall and only 17% has irrigation; even hardy crops such as agave suffer severe stress under precipitation below 600 mm/year.
  • Climate disasters and erosion: Droughts, late frosts, and floods cause recurring crop losses. Furthermore, 50% of soils present physical limitations and suffer severe erosion when left as bare soil on hillsides during intense storms.
  • Monoculture depletion and the spatial “last mile”: Repeating the same crop depletes nutrients and favors pests. Although NASA measures the planet's water and energy daily, its scientific formats (HDF5, NetCDF) remain inaccessible to the producer in the furrow.
  • In agronomic research, there is a certain limitation due to the wide variety of changes in specific zones, creating one of the major challenges.
  • Scarcity of ground truth: A satellite observes from hundreds of kilometers above and faces physical limitations: cloud cover blocks optical sensors such as Landsat, and a single SMAP pixel covers nearly $9\text{ km}^2$ where different crops, soil types, and microclimates are mixed.
  • Validation of spatial downscaling models: In complex terrain: One of the greatest methodological challenges for an Earth observation scientist is bringing regional-scale variables (SMAP moisture or GPM rainfall) down to the plot scale by intersecting them with topography (SRTM) and leaf/canopy temperature (ECOSTRESS/Landsat).
  • Longitudinal evidence on climate resilience and soil health: By linking farmer crop logs with historical records of vegetation vigor (Landsat/MODIS NDVI), crop residue cover (NDTI), and moisture (SMAP), researchers obtain empirical evidence on how regenerative rotations stabilize yields against droughts compared to monoculture.

3. The Solution: How Dr.Farm Turns Orbital Data into Action

Dr. Farm translates multi-layer NASA satellite telemetry into clear, operational plot-level recommendations:

  • Interactive 2D and 3D Hectare Mapping (Leaflet + Cesium): After authenticating, the user draws the boundary of their plot in 2D (Leaflet) or inspects slopes and real terrain relief in 3D (Cesium), automatically calculating the cultivated area and exporting the polygons in standard GeoJSON format interoperable with NASA Harvest.
  • Decision Engine: Cross-references recent rainfall density and intensity (GPM) with water infiltrated into the root zone (SMAP) and slope (SRTM). If a light rain did not wet the roots, it recommends irrigating; if recharge has already occurred, it suspends irrigation to save water and pumping energy.
  • PAR (400–700 nm), UV, and Water Vapor Monitoring: Evaluates light available for photosynthesis, warns of UV-B sunburn, and calculates Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD) to anticipate stomatal closure.
  • Vulnerability Alerts and Livestock Extension: Detects critical windows of erosive bare soil, heat waves, and frosts in low-lying areas, and integrates vigor monitoring in pastures and forages for mixed crop-livestock systems.

4. Use of NASA Data and Spatial Harmonization

Dr.Farm integrates visual WMS services from NASA GIBS / Earthdata with historical date controls alongside numerical time series processed in Python and Pandas. To bring regional sensors down to the plot scale, we apply spatial downscaling by intersecting SMAP moisture with 30 m SRTM relief and ECOSTRESS/Landsat surface temperature, in addition to fusing Landsat and MODIS to prevent cloud-cover gaps. Using farmer-provided data, we will estimate the water balance; otherwise, we will rely on official NASA data or data from a neighboring farmer to contribute those figures daily.

7. Technology Architecture of Artemis Squad

Developed under a collaborative multi-branch version control workflow (feature branching), the architecture integrates:

  • Frontend and Geovisualization (React + JavaScript + Leaflet + Cesium + Meteomatics): React and JavaScript interface combining Leaflet to draw hectare polygons in 2D and Cesium to visualize 3D terrain relief, consuming satellite mosaics via NASA Earthdata / GIBS WMS.
  • Backend and Data Science (Node.js + Python + Docker + Xarray): Node.js manages authentication and REST APIs, orchestrating Python microservices with Pandas that process NASA POWER and SMAP time series to execute the root-zone water balance.
  • Relational Database (SQL): SQL persistence for users, plot geometries, irrigation logs, and field reports.

8. Bidirectional Impact: Value for the Field and Open Science

  • Benefit to the Farmer: Saves water and pumping energy, prevents hillside erosion, and reduces losses from frost or heat.
  • Return to NASA (Citizen Science): Every delineated polygon, registered crop, and field confirmation contributes real agricultural boundaries, crop labels, and ground-truthing data to calibrate orbital algorithms.

Field Shift Guiding Principle: In Dr.Farm, satellite data and models are decision-support tools; they complement farm management with orbital evidence, but never replace the farmer’s empirical knowledge or local expert judgment.
